speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that that is generally approved. I do not see why it should not be, but silence would have been as good approval as this applause which I did not expect. And there is no greater friend of this country than he who will make it his cardinal principle, and will work day and night in support of that principle, to bring all sections of this country into accord, and, in the spirit of selfsacrifice which must be exercised by a nation as well as by an individual, to bear the burdens of to-day for the sake of the wealth, progress, unity, and power of the future,-bear	them even though the
shoulder may be galled and the back compelled to bend under those burdens. That was the spirit of the remarks made by my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden); I would like to have seen that spirit better and more thoroughly appreciated by the leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). He says to the leader of the opposition: We have been in power fifteen years, true; you have been in opposition fifteen years; what have you done to smooth away these divergences between the east and the west? Now', that is either a pertinent remark or an impertinent remark-I mean, impertinent in the old sense of being not pertinent. And the right hon. gentleman turns to his following of level-headed men and asks them to swallow a statement like that as an argument which they should applaud.
You, as leader of the opposition, have been there for fourteen years, what have you done to assuage those conditions? Well, does my hon. friend think that is a pertinent remark? Does Be think that an opposition, without the pow'er of carrying a single item of legislation, without the power of instituting a single reform, with only the power of protest and suggestion; because he, during his fifteen years, has done little Mr. FOSTER.
to assuage that condition, does he think he has answered the case against himself when he asks what the opposition has done during that fifteen years? The leader of the opposition and the opposition itself have tried to do much which would have made the west better off than it is to-day. The leader of the opposition and the men behind him stood for an unshackled sisterhood of provinces in the Northwest, with all the powers that their elder sisters possess, with all the powers that the British North America Act conferred upon them. And who shackled that sisterhood of provinces, shackled them for ever, so far as he could? He sits there as the leader of the government. The leader of the opposition and the men acting with him on this side of the House tried their best, w'hen those provinces were set apart with slender means, to give them the most favourable start in the work of progress and advancement. My hon. friend and his coadjutors on this side of the House tried to put within the power of those provinces the great natural franchises that were theirs by nature and theirs by neighbourhood, and which they should have been allowed to operate. That they did not get their lands, or their forests, or anything else of those dowers of nature, is due to. the fact that the right hon. gentleman who leads this House decreed that it should not be done. Then exploiters, and grafters, and land hunters were carrying out their delectable operations in the interests of their country and for the public good in those Northwest provinces. The leader of the opposition and his co-helpers Qn this side of the House were doing the' best they could to their progress to hunt them out, *and to preserve for the Northwest all that it was possible to preserve as a trust to be conserved for the good of the country, and not for the wealth of the spoilers. Whilst that operation was going on year after year, my right hon. friend, who is so testy in his temper to-night, stood straight behind every grafter, and every land hunter, and every backstairs man who wanted to get the people's patrimony for nothing. That they were successful and got it, is not due to any co-operation on this side of the House, but to the protection given them by my right hon. friend. These are some of the things that the leader of the opposition and his followers have been trying to do for the Northwest. Does my right hon. friend think now that that was a pertinent remark, that he had answered everything, everything, when he put me question as to what the members of the opposition had done towards the amelioration of the Northwest? Well, my right hon. friend left the Northwest, and I am told that he did not leave the Northwest in very good temper. Perhaps that had something to do with the testy nature of his remarks to-night.

He then took up the tariff. With my right hon. friend the tariff is a very hot instrument, and he dropped it almost immediately, with the sage remark that he did not intend to go very deeply into the subject. I appreciated that remark, I appreciated the state of mind of my right hon. friend when he made that remark, if he thought back for a little. The query which arose in my mind was this: Suppose my right hon. friend had attempted to go very deep into the tariff, where in the world would he have come out? We have memories, history has not vacated this country of Canada. We remember ourselves, and if we do not we can brush up our history, and find out the devious wanderings of my right hon. friend on this matter of the tariff and the fiscal position of the Dominion of Canada. Shall 1 recall a few of them? My right hon. friend did not care to go into it very deeply, may I assist him? How many years was he wandering through this sandy desert, setting up false gods, and bowing down to the golden calves of continental free trade, of commercial union, of unrestricted reciprocity, and of discrimination against the mother country, to which he is so effusively loyal to-night? How many years was he wandering there, worshipping first one, then throwing it aside, worshipping a second with even greater ardour and throwing that aside, then bowing down on all fours before a third one, and worshipping that with still greater fervour? No wonder my right hon. friend does not care to go very deeply into the tariff.
Then he may have pictured himself in the city of London, in the province of Ontario, at a certain time before the elections of 1896, when, in order to go Sir Charles Tupper one better, he pledged his word of honour as a man and as leader of his party, that if he got into power he would immediately send a delegation to England, and try to get what he had lauded as a very great benefit to this country, namely, mutual preference between Great Britain and Canada, on the lines of Mr. Chamberlain's proposition. Does he rememebr that episode, and does he remember, too, when he stood before this House and this country and declared that they had redeemed their promises, that instead of attempting to redeem that promise which he made on his honour as a man, he went over to Great Britain and the very first time he mounted a platform he declared to that country: We do mot want any return preference from you ; we are going to give you something, but we will give it as a free gift; protection is a bane, a curse ; do not put it upon the necks of the people of Great Britain. Does the right hon. gentleman remember that? If he had gone deeply into this matter of the tariff would he have retraced the history of himself in that transaction?
He has brought up to-night the question
of 1891, when the Liberal-Conservative government was not too proud to seek for reciprocity at Washington. That was somewhat of an unfortunate reminiscence for the right hon. gentleman. It shows two cardinal differences between him and the party he leads and Liberal-Conservatism and the party that the Liberal-Conservatives lead. We did not go down to Washington in 1891 to negotiate for a treaty of reciprocity until we had appealed to the country, told them that we were going and got their mandate for going. To-day the right hon. gentleman proposes to conclude, if he can, a treaty of reaiprocity with the United States of America as to which he has not asked a mandate and for which the country has given him absolutely no instructions at all. But worse than that for my hon. friend ; when he went to the country in 1904 and when he went to the country in 1908, he went with these words on his lips : I do not think that Canada wishes for reciprocity with the United States of America. There was a time when I was anxious for it, and would have given anything for it, but to-day I do not think Canada wants it; as for me I have turned my back on Washington and I have set my face -towards England. I ask the right hon. gentleman if, with these words on his lips passing up and down this country appealing to the people on political platforms, I am not justified in saying that the mandate he got in 1904 and 1908 was to leave reciprocity with the United States alone and to devote his superabundant energies to the cultivation of better trade relations with Great Britain and the empire of which we form a part.
More, Sir, I will refresh my hon. friend's memory, as long as he did not wish to go deeply into the tariff, on another point. We went to Washington in 1891, we met their men, we talked over the matter of trade relations and after a long series of conferences we came to the final conference in which Mr. Secretary Blaine, who spoke for the United States, said to us : We are willing to trade with your country on a better footing than to-day ; we are willing to give you in our country certain reductions on natural products and on manufactured goods, but we will give them on one condition and one condition alone ; that is that you should discriminate against Great Britain in our favour and so confirm us in your market to the extent of the reductions which you make on manufactured goods. That is the demand plainly stated. We will treat with you on a reciprocal basis, but it must be on the understanding that you will give us a better footing in your market than you give Great Britain. That was the proposition made to us. We thanked Mr. Blaine for the proposition, but we told him that it was absolutely imposible to con-

ing to him, and puts up a fence, in this case a commission, which may last till the next election is over and hold out this promise of future betterment-that is, unless the Northwest farmers are less keen than I think them to be. But to my mind they will be hard-headed enough to say to themselves: 1894 taught us a lesson, and in 1910 we have the same old jollying; but before he goes to the country, we will get a categorical answer out of him, yes or no. That I think will be the spirit of the Northwest. But my right hon. friend was not enamoured of commissions in 1895. Does he remember his speech in Toronto in that year, when he was seeking for power, and when he despised commissions, ridiculed them, spoke of them in the most sarcastic terms, and declared: Put us in; we will revise your tariff; we know exactly what the country needs, and we will give the country what it needs. When he got into power he found that he did not know as much as he thought he did about the country, and he had recourse to commissions, and he has had recourse to commissions since, and I suppose he will continue to have recourse to commissions.
A word or two, Mr. Speaker, with reference to the after-dinner remarks of my right hon. friend. He declared that he would not follow the leader of the opposition in much ' of the matter which was -referred to by my hon. friend. The large matter which was referred to strongly by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was the matter of public administration in this Canada of ours. That is a most important matter. I am not guilty of saying what is not absolutely true when I say that alongside _ of honest, decent, respectable administration in this country, reciprocity is not in it at all. The question of administration to-day is, I believe, the most important, vital question with "which we have to deal and with which the people of this country have to deal. The arraignment of my right hon. friend by the leader of the opposition this afternoon was one which demanded an answer at the hands of my right hon. Mend. It. was a powerful impeachment of him and his ministers as trustees for the people blocking every attempt on the part of the people to find out how their money had been expended-blocking it in the face of humiliating exposes and scandals without number proved to. the hilt. My right hon. friend had no answer to that; he said he would not follow the leader of the opposition in that respect. He would have done better to have met that charge the red-hot instant that it was made. The people will do their own thinking, when a man who ' leads a government has it put up to him as it was put up to him "this afternoon, and has not a word to say. but promises in a sort of indefinite way that at some time or other he will take it up and discuss it. But Mr. FOSTER.
he was not so punctilious with reference to another question that could have been just as well discussed on another day as it was to-day-the question of reciprocity. And so he made the statement that the question of reciprocity was the most important and urgent in the Dominion of Canada to-day. Will my right hon. friend pardon me one remark? If the question of reciprocity is exciting any interest to-day in this country, it is due solely to the fact that my right hon. friend, without mandate or warrant from the people, nas undertaken to change our fiscal basis and to bring about some arrangement which will affect every business and every great interest in this country. That is the only reason why there is any interest in the matter, and it is an interest prompted by trembling and fear. Would I be considered impertinent if I asked my hon. friend what warrant he had from the country for undertaking reciprocity negotiations? If I should ask him to lay on the table all the requests that have come in the shape of petitions from boards of trade, associations or corporations of any kind, or from individuals, begging him to hasten a treaty of reciprocity with the United States, how many documents could he produce? Could he furnish half a dozen? Where did he get his mandate for disturbing every financial interest in this country, for running counter to his own express statement of two years ago, and traversing the policy of independent Canadian development which we have been following for the past 25 years. Surely my right hon. friend should give some answer to that question. Either there is or there is not a demand in this country for reciprocity. Will my right hon. friend indicate whence the demand comes and lay on the table any documents which -will show any such demand? I have most diligently sought for indications of Canadian opinion in that matter, and to my mind the trend of public opinion in Canada is absolutely opposed to any reciprocity treaty with the United States. _	_
There is another question which I think pertinent, and that is as to the opportuneness of the time and of the conditions for entering into reciprocity negotiations. When one looks dispassionately over the ground, it would seem that the time and the conditions are absolutely inopportune for any such negotiations. If there be not good trade relations between us and the United States, there is absolutely good feeling and friendliness. I object most emphatically to the dictum laid down by the right' hon. gentleman that free trade relations are essential to the existence of friendly intercourse between different nations. Honest, upright dealing I grant is absolutely necessary, but free trade is not. Free trade relations may make for still warmer friendliness, but the man who has no right upon you cannot feel aggrieved if you stand by

our own rights and say to him I am your friend as you are mine, but my policy is in this direction, and I cannot admit you to a share in it. No reasonable man could take objection to that ground, but let me ask, if the trade relations between the iwo countries are to-day unsatisfactory, on whose side is the fault? Perhaps I might refresh my hon. friend's memory. What do I find in the last records of the United States? I find that the duties on dutiable goods in different years were as follows:

Now take the Canadian duty upon dutiable goods. During all those years it did not exceed an average of 28 per cent. Are the negotiations proceeding on this basis? Are they proceeding on the basis of our telling our neighbours that they have not given us a fair deal, that they have practically prohibited our trade, and that while they have done all they could to prevent our goods going into their country, the duty we charge upon American goods is lower to day than it was some years ago? But the story is not all told by the general duty. Here are some figures with reference to the groups of articles. Animals going from Canada into the United States have to pay an average duty of 25.23 per cent.; bread tuffs 32.65; manufactures of cotton 52.41; iron and steel manufactures 38 per cent.; leather manufactures 36.27; meat and dairy products \34i56; sugar and .confectionery 60.36; vegetables 40 per cent.; woollen manufactures 90i per cent.
Those are the duties that meet us when we bring our exports up to the United States borders. Now contrast our tariff with theirs. For the last 25 years to go back no further, we have been levying on their goods a tariff about one-half the rate which they imposed upon ours. Does my right hon. friend think that we are responsible for the lack of freer trade relations? But what is to be said of the common sense of undertaking reciprocity negotiations with a country which is just changing its politcal control, and in which the party which is about to take possession of the White House has, as its cardinal principle the lowering of the duties imposed by the United States upon foreign goods, especially upon raw materials, foods, bread stuffs and the like. When conditions are in likelihood of being changed by the country which in all good faith, ought to change them because their duties have been so unneighbourly
high, when the whole trend of political opinion in the United States is running in that direction, why, in the name of common sense, if there is no mandate from our people, cannot we wait in patience until we see the result of this struggle and know which party to that struggle is to be in control.
It does seem to me, taking all these things into consideration, that it has been an imprudent thing, to say the least, for my right hon. friend to undertake these negotiations. Why were they promised in 1910? It was not a neighbourly act when the United States, in February, 1910, notwithstanding the treatment given us by them and the treatment given them by us, to raise the big stick and flourish it over Canada threatening that, even after the long continuance of such unfair conditions, they would fine us 25 per cent of the value of our dutiable goods going into their country unless we gave them more. That was enough to show my right hon. friend the attitude of the United States and to enable him to judge whether that country was animated by the most neighbourly and friendly sentiments toward us. I do not think that such action does manifest a neighbourly spirit. I should like to see some fruits mete for repentance brought forth before quite trusting the .good feeling in this matter of those in control of the administration of the United States.
I do not propose to follow this further, except to make one remark: trade is one thing, nationality is another. There are strange and mysterious relations, however, between trade with its tariffs and nationality. The time often comes when trade must be burdened for the sake of nationality and that burden bonie with equanimity, aye, and with ardour. I would urge my right hon. friend to remember that, for twenty-five years we have been putting our hands deep in our pockets, we have been spending our treasure and our energy without stint, to build up a progressive and permanent nationality. And it does not consist with that policy and that self-sacrifice that, at this particular juncture, we should entangle ourselves in a binding and formal treaty with the United States. My right hon. friend made the statement that he was going to give us much light on the subject of how they were carrying on these negotiations. And the light he gave us was the statement that one principle laid down was that there should be no interference with the British preference. I have heard my right hon. friend say that before, and I have seen him whittling away at the British preference as industriously as a mischievous school boy at his school desk. No interference with the British preference? Why, your French treaty shore away a part of it. No interference with the British preference? Your capitulation to the big stick

last year whittled off another part of it. No interference with the British preference? Your gift to Holland and Belgium for nought in return whittled away a portion of the British preference. And Holland, after having received this gift at your hands, decides to adopt a protective tariff and will very soon tax *' your goods that go into that market. Your arrangement with Italy helped to interfere with the British tariff. Your arrangement with France had not to do with France only; it let in twelve or fifteen countries on the same basis and to that extent whittled away still more of the British preference. With these assertions made by the Prime Minister year after year, and with the record of performance standing opposite to them, I confess I am a little doubtful as to whether he would stand by this latest utterance of his about not interfering with the British preference. Sir, within the last twenty years changes have taken place in this empire, changes which have come about with astonishing rapidity, changes which have not yet all matured but which are all in the line of co-operation between the various parts of the empire and of progressive and helpful work for the expansion of trade, the extension of means of communication, the placing of capital and the building up of industry. Even within the last ten years there have been such strides forward on the part of the British Empire in this direction as would have astonished any man had they been prophesied to him ten years ago. And, so far as Canada is concerned, what is the trend? East and west carriage for the products of Canada and for what comes in and for what goes out; our own seaports to handle our imports and exports; our own subsidiary occupations and pursuits to cluster about the great east and west transportation; our own mills to grind our wheat; our own labour to make up what we want ; our own capital and capital that becomes Canadian to give power to the arm of the labourer. That is the ideal toward which Canada has been working. And, that being the case, I view with apprehension any entanglements of a binding and formal treaty which will tend by a single iota to interfere with that policy which, I believe, was properly conceived and has been nobly carried out so far and upon which our future so greatly depends. A cent a pound more on butter, a cent a pound more on cream, two or three cents more on wheat- all that is something and I appreciate the force of such an argument. But the nationality that we are building up with selfsacrifice and with all the power that we possess and with the expenditure of an immensity of money is something more even than the profits of trade. In the end the great benefit for us lies in the other direc-Mr. FOSTER.
tion. In that other direction are our friends, our own people. They have given us our liberties ; they have protected us ; their children have gone out to the uttermost parts of the earth and with us are building up subsidiary nations within the empire. Surely we are safer in the hands of our friends and relatives than we -are in the hands of strangers. With these considerations, which I cannot help bringing to the front, I voice my apprehension, and I voice more than my apprehension, I voice my opposition, in so far as I can see into this matter, to any formal treaty with the United States. Keep this legislature absolutely free to do as it likes in this connection. Do we know what two years will bring forth ? This is a day of rapid development in Canada. No one knows what ten years may bring forth. Why, after we have gained these powers and rights, should we put hobbles about our limbs and manacles about our hands? There are other considerations deeper yet, and which will probably be brought out before this session is over, which incline me to be apprehensive with reference to this matter. If you want better trade relations with the United States, persuade them to give us fair tariffs for our fair tariffs. Let them make their tariffs and conserve their liberties; then let us make our tariffs and conserve our liberties. But why in God's name tie ourselves up by a ten years' treaty with the trusts, and combinations, and mighty industrial powers and interests of the United States of America? I do not know, and I cannot find a satisfactory answer. Mr. Sneaker, I was going to say something with reference to the navy, but I will defer that to another time.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: As the hour is late, I merely rise to move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, House adjourned at 10.10 p.m.
Tuesday, November 22, 1910.
